new.title: Climb to the roof of the Arc de Triomphe
new.desc: Napoleon's triumphal arch stands in the middle of a star of twelve avenues, and from the roof terrace you see them all fan out, with the Champs-Élysées running straight down to Concorde. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier lies under the vault.
new.tip: Never cross the roundabout on foot: take the underpass from the Champs-Élysées side. Go near dusk to watch the avenue lights come on.
new.q: Arc de Triomphe, Place Charles de Gaulle, Paris

new.title: Hunt for the follies of Parc Monceau
new.desc: This English-style park is ringed by grand mansions and dotted with make-believe ruins and miniature monuments, leftovers of an 18th-century duke's fantasy garden. It is where the smart 8th arrondissement comes to jog, read and picnic.
new.tip: Enter through the gilded gates by the rotunda at Monceau metro and loop round to the colonnade by the pond.
new.q: Parc Monceau, Paris

new.title: Wander the Petit Palais for free
new.desc: Built for the 1900 World Fair, the Petit Palais is the City of Paris fine arts museum, and its permanent collection costs nothing to see. The building itself, all mosaics, ironwork and painted ceilings, is half the show.
new.tip: Head for the inner courtyard garden with its colonnade and café: a calm hideout a few steps from the Champs-Élysées.
new.q: Petit Palais, Avenue Winston Churchill, Paris

new.title: Face the Eiffel Tower from the Trocadéro
new.desc: The esplanade between the two wings of the Palais de Chaillot gives the most famous head-on view of the Eiffel Tower, with the Trocadéro gardens and their big fountain at your feet.
new.tip: Come early in the morning, before the crowds and the souvenir sellers, then walk down through the gardens towards the river.
new.q: Esplanade du Trocadéro, Paris

new.title: Find Guimard's Castel Béranger
new.desc: Before he drew the Métro entrances, Hector Guimard designed this apartment block, the first Art Nouveau residence in Paris, down to the ironwork and door handles. It won the city's façade competition in 1898.
new.tip: The flats are private, so admire the swirling entrance gate from the pavement, then continue along Rue Jean de la Fontaine to spot the Hôtel Mezzara at number 60.
new.q: Castel Béranger, 14 Rue Jean de la Fontaine, Paris

new.title: Step inside Le Corbusier's Maison La Roche
new.desc: Hidden at the end of a private lane in Auteuil, this white 1920s villa was built for a Swiss banker and his avant-garde art collection. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage list and now belongs to the Fondation Le Corbusier.
new.tip: Walk up the curved ramp in the gallery to feel the 'architectural promenade' the house was designed around. Check opening days before you go.
new.q: Maison La Roche, 10 Square du Docteur Blanche, Paris

new.title: See the painting that named Impressionism
new.desc: The Musée Marmottan Monet, a former hunting lodge by the Bois de Boulogne, keeps Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' along with hundreds of his other works and the world's largest public collection of Berthe Morisot.
new.tip: Go down to the basement gallery for the late water lilies, then stroll through the Jardin du Ranelagh outside. The nearest metro is La Muette.
new.q: Musée Marmottan Monet, 2 Rue Louis Boilly, Paris

new.title: Stroll down the Cité des Fleurs
new.desc: A private lane laid out in 1847 in the Épinettes quarter, where every house had to keep a front garden and matching stone vases on the wall. Sisley lived at number 27 and a plaque at number 25 recalls a Resistance forgery workshop.
new.tip: The gates are open to walkers during the day and close in the evening and on Sunday afternoons. Brochant metro is closest.
new.q: Cité des Fleurs, Paris 17e

new.title: Circle Gehry's glass ship in the Bois
new.desc: The Fondation Louis Vuitton, designed by Frank Gehry, looks like a ship of billowing glass sails moored at the edge of the Bois de Boulogne. Inside are big exhibitions of 20th and 21st century art.
new.tip: Climb to the roof terraces for views over the treetops, and book a timed ticket ahead for the blockbuster shows.
new.q: Fondation Louis Vuitton, 8 Avenue du Mahatma Gandhi, Paris

new.title: Pick macarons at Ladurée on the Champs-Élysées
new.desc: The famous macaron house runs a tea room, bar and restaurant on the avenue, with a pastry counter in pastel colours. Pricey, but a Paris classic.
new.tip: Skip the table queue: buy a small box at the counter and eat them on a bench further down the avenue.
new.q: Ladurée, 75 Avenue des Champs-Élysées, Paris

new.title: Have tea under a Tiepolo ceiling
new.desc: Le Nélie, the tea room of the Musée Jacquemart-André, sits in the old dining room of a Boulevard Haussmann mansion, beneath a ceiling fresco brought over from a villa near Venice. Pastries, teas and a few dishes that nod to the current exhibition.
new.tip: You can come for the tea room alone without a museum ticket. There is a covered terrace too.
new.q: Musée Jacquemart-André, 158 Boulevard Haussmann, Paris

new.title: Linger over cake at Carette
new.desc: This pâtisserie and salon de thé on the Place du Trocadéro is a 16th arrondissement institution for pastries, salads and people-watching on the terrace.
new.tip: A good reward after the Trocadéro view. Weekends get busy, so try a weekday morning.
new.q: Carette, 4 Place du Trocadéro, Paris

new.title: Graze the Marché Président Wilson
new.desc: Twice a week this chic market fills the avenue in front of the Palais de Tokyo with fish, game, cheese and rare vegetables. Unusually for Paris, it also has lots of hot food to take away, from crêpes to rotisserie chicken.
new.tip: It runs on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Walk the whole length once before buying, then eat your finds within sight of the Seine. Metro Iéna.
new.q: Marché Président Wilson, Avenue du Président Wilson, Paris

new.title: Shop the Batignolles organic market
new.desc: Every Saturday, producers set up on the central strip of the Boulevard des Batignolles to sell their own organic fruit, cheese, jam and wine. You can also eat on the spot: quiches, soups and tarts made by the stallholders.
new.tip: Saturday only. Come before noon, then carry your picnic to the Square des Batignolles. Metro Rome is at the market's doorstep.
new.q: Marché biologique des Batignolles, Boulevard des Batignolles, Paris

new.title: Queue for steak-frites at Le Relais de Venise
new.desc: Since 1959 this Porte Maillot restaurant has served one thing only: walnut salad, then sliced entrecôte with fries and a secret butter sauce, brought in two helpings. Locals simply call it 'L'Entrecôte'.
new.tip: No bookings are taken, so expect a queue on the pavement. Arrive just before opening and keep room for the profiteroles.
new.q: Le Relais de Venise, 271 Boulevard Pereire, Paris

new.title: Drink a glass at Les Caves Populaires
new.desc: A friendly, unfussy wine bar on lively Rue des Dames in the Batignolles, full of regulars at old wooden tables. Wine by the glass, simple cheese and charcuterie boards, and chess if you fancy a game.
new.tip: Seats are hard to find later in the evening, so arrive early and grab the spot by the big front window.
new.q: Les Caves Populaires, 22 Rue des Dames, Paris

new.title: Row a boat on the Lac Inférieur
new.desc: The largest lake in the Bois de Boulogne was dug in the 1850s and has rowing boats for hire from spring to autumn. In the middle is an island with a little kiosk built for Napoleon III.
new.tip: Walk in from the La Muette side of the park. Afterwards follow the shore to the Grande Cascade, where you can step into the grottoes behind the waterfall.
new.q: Lac Inférieur, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

new.title: Smell the roses at Bagatelle
new.desc: The little château of Bagatelle was built in just over two months in 1777 to win a bet with Marie Antoinette. Its park in the Bois de Boulogne holds a rose garden with thousands of plants, plus an iris garden and a water lily pond.
new.tip: June is the moment: the roses peak and the international new rose competition is held here. Bring a picnic, as the park is far from any metro.
new.q: Parc de Bagatelle, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

new.title: Warm up in the Serres d'Auteuil
new.desc: A botanical garden of turquoise cast-iron greenhouses from the 1890s, with a steamy palm house, orchids and a formal French garden in front. Next door, a Roland-Garros tennis court is itself wrapped in greenhouses.
new.tip: Perfect on a cold grey day, when the tropical house feels like another continent. Metro Porte d'Auteuil.
new.q: Jardin des Serres d'Auteuil, Avenue de la Porte d'Auteuil, Paris

new.title: Ride the rides at the Jardin d'Acclimatation
new.desc: Opened in 1860 at the northern tip of the Bois de Boulogne, this is one of the oldest amusement parks anywhere: gentle rides, a miniature train, ponies and a Guignol puppet theatre. A favourite Parisian childhood memory.
new.tip: Best with young children. Combine it with the Fondation Louis Vuitton, which stands right beside it.
new.q: Jardin d'Acclimatation, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

new.title: Picnic in Parc Martin Luther King
new.desc: The biggest park in the 17th was laid out on old railway land in the new Clichy-Batignolles district. Locals come to run, play sport, picnic and enjoy the blossom in spring.
new.tip: Pick up food at the Saturday organic market or on Rue des Batignolles and walk over. Pont Cardinet station is at the gate.
new.q: Parc Clichy-Batignolles Martin Luther King, 147 Rue Cardinet, Paris

new.title: Walk the old railway of the Petite Ceinture
new.desc: Between La Muette and Porte d'Auteuil, a disused stretch of Paris's ring railway has become a wild nature trail of over a kilometre, with meadow, woodland and the old ballast still underfoot.
new.tip: Start at the Jardin du Ranelagh, where a piece of rail survives at the entrance, and walk south. The main section closes at night like other city parks.
new.q: Petite Ceinture du 16e, Paris

new.title: Meet the kings of France in Saint-Denis
new.desc: The choir of the Basilique de Saint-Denis, finished in 1144, is where Gothic architecture began. It is also the royal necropolis: nearly every French king is buried here, among them Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette.
new.tip: Metro line 13 stops right by it at Basilique de Saint-Denis. Outside, look for the workshop rebuilding the spire that was taken down in the 19th century.
new.q: Basilique de Saint-Denis, Saint-Denis

new.title: Board a Concorde at Le Bourget
new.desc: The Musée de l'Air et de l'Espace, on the edge of Le Bourget airport, shows around 150 aircraft, from early flying machines to rockets. You can walk through two Concordes and a Boeing 747.
new.tip: Bus 152 from Porte de la Villette stops outside. The permanent collection is free on the first Sunday of the month.
new.q: Musée de l'Air et de l'Espace, Le Bourget

new.title: Get lost in the Puces de Saint-Ouen
new.desc: Just beyond the ring road in Saint-Ouen lies what is billed as the world's largest antiques market: about fifteen markets and nearly 2,000 dealers, from the jumble of Vernaison to the grand furniture of Paul-Bert and Serpette.
new.tip: It runs Saturday to Monday. From Porte de Clignancourt, ignore the cheap stalls under the ring road and keep walking to Rue des Rosiers. Mind your pockets.
new.q: Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen, Rue des Rosiers, Saint-Ouen

new.title: Lunch to gypsy jazz at La Chope des Puces
new.desc: This small bistro in the Saint-Ouen flea market is a shrine to jazz manouche, watched over by the spirit of Django Reinhardt, with guitars of famous players on the walls. The kitchen does French classics like boeuf bourguignon and blanquette.
new.tip: The guitarists play on Saturday and Sunday afternoons. The room is tiny, so come early or be ready to stand at the bar.
new.q: La Chope des Puces, 122 Rue des Rosiers, Saint-Ouen

new.title: Eat your way round the Saint-Denis market
new.desc: One of the busiest markets in the Paris region spreads through an 1893 iron hall and the streets around it, a short walk from the basilica. Stallholders and shoppers come from all over the world, and so does the food.
new.tip: Market days are Tuesday, Friday and Sunday. Sunday morning is the liveliest; combine it with the basilica.
new.q: Marché de Saint-Denis, Rue Gabriel Péri, Saint-Denis

new.title: Follow the Canal de l'Ourcq through Pantin
new.desc: Pantin's old industrial canal bank has turned into an arts quarter: the Magasins Généraux customs warehouses, the huge former flour mill of the Grands Moulins and the Centre National de la Danse all line the towpath. Street art covers the walls along the way.
new.tip: Walk or cycle out from Parc de la Villette along the towpath. The dance centre's rooftop and canteen are open to visitors. Metro Église de Pantin brings you back.
new.q: Magasins Généraux, 1 Rue de l'Ancien Canal, Pantin

new.title: Explore the peach walls of Montreuil
new.desc: Montreuil once had hundreds of kilometres of plastered walls that soaked up the sun to ripen peaches for the royal court and even the Russian tsars. A few hectares of this maze, the Murs à pêches, survive and are being replanted by volunteers.
new.tip: The garden plots are run by local associations and open on certain days, often weekend afternoons, so check their calendar first. The entrance is on Impasse Gobétue.
new.q: Murs à pêches, Impasse Gobétue, Montreuil

new.title: Climb the keep of the Château de Vincennes
new.desc: A real medieval fortress at the end of metro line 1: its 14th-century keep, some 50 metres high, was the tallest in Europe. Henry V of England died here, and Diderot and the Marquis de Sade were locked up inside.
new.tip: Don't miss the Sainte-Chapelle across the courtyard, a one-level cousin of the one in Paris. The Bois de Vincennes starts just behind the walls.
new.q: Château de Vincennes, Vincennes

new.title: Dance at the guinguette Chez Gégène
new.desc: On the bank of the Marne in Joinville-le-Pont, Chez Gégène is the most famous of the old guinguettes, the riverside dance halls where Parisians spent their Sundays. Traditional cooking on the terrace by the water, and an orchestra for the dancers.
new.tip: Go for Saturday evening or Sunday lunch, when the band plays, and check the dance calendar first. It is a walk across the bridge from Joinville-le-Pont RER station.
new.q: Chez Gégène, 162 bis Quai de Polangis, Joinville-le-Pont

new.title: Eat on an island in the Marne
new.desc: The Guinguette de l'Île du Martin-Pêcheur in Champigny-sur-Marne has a whole wooded island to itself. There is live music, room to dance and games for children under the trees.
new.tip: Book ahead for sunny weekends and check which evenings have a band. Champigny RER station is the nearest.
new.q: Guinguette de l'Île du Martin-Pêcheur, 41 Quai Victor Hugo, Champigny-sur-Marne

new.title: Spend an afternoon at the MAC VAL
new.desc: Vitry-sur-Seine is home to a large museum devoted to art made in France since the 1950s, with works by Buren, Soulages and Tinguely, a cinema and a public garden around it. It is a bold piece of culture in the southern suburbs.
new.tip: Tram T9 from Porte de Choisy has a stop named after the museum. Vitry is also known for its street art, so keep your eyes on the walls on the way.
new.q: MAC VAL, Place de la Libération, Vitry-sur-Seine

new.title: See 3,000 kinds of rose in L'Haÿ-les-Roses
new.desc: The Roseraie du Val-de-Marne was started in the 1890s by Jules Gravereaux, a Bon Marché department store man with a passion for roses. Today some 13,000 bushes of around 3,200 varieties grow in formal beds and over arches, and the town even took its name from them.
new.tip: The garden only opens in the rose season, with the peak in June. Take RER B to Bourg-la-Reine and a bus from there.
new.q: Roseraie du Val-de-Marne, L'Haÿ-les-Roses

new.title: Follow Van Gogh's last steps in Auvers-sur-Oise
new.desc: Van Gogh spent his final weeks painting in this village on the Oise. The church he made famous still stands above the main street, and a path through the wheat fields leads to the cemetery where he and his brother Theo lie side by side.
new.tip: On weekends from April to October a direct train runs from Gare du Nord; otherwise change on the way. From the church, walk uphill to the cemetery.
new.q: Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, Auvers-sur-Oise

new.title: Dine at Van Gogh's inn, the Auberge Ravoux
new.desc: Van Gogh lodged and died in a tiny attic room of this inn opposite the town hall of Auvers-sur-Oise. Downstairs, the restored dining room where he ate serves dishes inspired by 19th-century regional cooking.
new.tip: Reserve a table and visit room number 5 upstairs first. The inn closes over the winter, so check dates before travelling.
new.q: Auberge Ravoux, Place de la Mairie, Auvers-sur-Oise

new.title: Walk the cloister of Royaumont Abbey
new.desc: Built in the 13th century with the backing of Saint Louis, the Cistercian abbey of Royaumont near Asnières-sur-Oise kept its cloister and vaulted refectory when the church was pulled down. It is now a cultural foundation with gardens and concerts; Pink Floyd played here in 1971.
new.tip: The nearest station is Viarmes on line H from Gare du Nord, a few kilometres away, so plan a taxi, a bike or a long country walk.
new.q: Abbaye de Royaumont, Asnières-sur-Oise

new.title: Visit the Renaissance château of Écouen
new.desc: Anne de Montmorency's 16th-century château on a hill north of Paris houses the national Renaissance museum. The star is the David and Bathsheba tapestry series, ten pieces running some 75 metres, once bought by Henry VIII.
new.tip: Take line H from Gare du Nord to Écouen-Ézanville, then walk up through the woods to the château. The terrace looks out over the plain.
new.q: Château d'Écouen, Musée national de la Renaissance, Écouen

new.title: Promenade by the lake in Enghien-les-Bains
new.desc: Enghien is a spa town with a lake, a casino and a touch of the seaside, only a short train ride north of Paris. The lakeside jetty has Art Nouveau lamps and old plane trees, and pedal boats dot the water.
new.tip: Hire a pedal boat in fine weather, or walk round the lake and look for the few gardens that open onto the water. Trains run from Gare du Nord on line H.
new.q: Lac d'Enghien, Enghien-les-Bains

new.title: Spend a beach day at L'Isle-Adam
new.desc: The pretty town of L'Isle-Adam on the Oise has a proper river beach, the largest in the Paris region, with sand, swimming and boats and pedalos to hire. A slice of old-fashioned seaside an hour from the city.
new.tip: It is a summer-only outing. Take line H to L'Isle-Adam Parmain station and cross the bridges over the Oise into town.
new.q: Plage de L'Isle-Adam, L'Isle-Adam
